title: Jaipur Couple Builds ₹2.4 Crore Organic Farm With 100 Gir Cows
excerpt: Vibhor and Ishita Jain turned a ₹20-25 lakh investment into Kinaya Organic Farms, producing A2 Gir cow milk, hand-churned ghee, and wood-pressed oils across a 12-acre property outside Jaipur.
body:
• Kinaya Organic Farms, run by Vibhor and Ishita Jain near Jaipur, generates ₹18-20 lakh in monthly revenue from 100 purebred Gir cows — approximately ₹2.16 to ₹2.4 crore annually.
  • The farm produces 250-300 litres of A2 Gir cow milk daily, priced at ₹150 per litre, along with hand-churned ghee at ₹3,490 per litre.
  • Started in 2018 with an investment of ₹20-25 lakh and 20 cows, the farm has expanded to include 2,000 trees, a biogas digester, and a circular organic system.
  • The venture taps into India's fast-growing A2 milk market, where consumers are willing to pay premium prices for indigenous breed dairy products.

Vibhor Jain studied computer science. He chose cows instead of code. Along with his wife Ishita, he now runs Kinaya Organic Farms, a 12-acre property about 35 kilometres from Jaipur that houses 100 purebred Gir cows and generates up to ₹2.4 crore in annual revenue.

From 20 Cows to a Full-Scale Operation

The couple launched the farm in 2018 with no family background in agriculture. Vibhor's interest in indigenous cattle drew him to Gujarat's Kathiawar region, where he spent time learning about the Gir breed from generational breeders.

"Around that time, his family happened to keep a couple of cows at home, despite having no agricultural or cow-farming background. That became his first exposure to cattle."

— Vibhor Jain, speaking to Startup Pedia

He started with 20 purebred Gir cows and one breeding bull, investing ₹20-25 lakh in training, livestock, and initial setup. After an initial trial period, the Jains moved to a larger permanent property and began scaling. The farm now spans 12 acres with 100 Gir cows, over 2,000 trees — including more than 500 mango trees across 40 varieties and 300 white sandalwood trees — plus seasonal vegetables and green fodder grown between the tree rows.

The A2 Milk Premium

The farm's 100 Gir cows produce 250-300 litres of milk daily. About 30-35% is sold as fresh milk at ₹150 per litre, while the remaining milk goes into value-added products — primarily hand-churned A2 ghee priced at ₹3,490 per litre. The farm produces approximately 9 litres of ghee daily, along with colostrum powder, milk powder, and wood-pressed oils.

These prices reflect a growing market reality in India: consumers, particularly in urban centres, are increasingly willing to pay several times the retail price for milk and ghee from indigenous breeds. The A2 milk movement — built on the claim that milk from desi breeds like Gir contains the A2 beta-casein protein, which some research suggests is easier to digest — has transformed indigenous dairy farming from a low-margin subsistence activity into a premium consumer category.

Circular Farming Model

Kinaya operates a closed-loop system. Cow dung is processed through a biogas digester, and the resulting slurry serves as organic fertiliser for the crops and fodder grown on-site. This reduces dependence on external inputs and keeps operating costs manageable — a critical factor given that each Gir cow produces only 8-10 litres daily, far less than commercial Jersey or Holstein breeds.

The farm also generates revenue from livestock sales, though the monthly ₹18-20 lakh figure represents product sales alone.

What It Means for Indian Dairy

India is the world's largest milk producer, but the dairy sector has long been dominated by high-yield crossbreeds and cooperative models focused on volume. Ventures like Kinaya represent a counter-trend: smaller-scale, premium-priced, direct-to-consumer operations built around indigenous breeds and organic practices.

For the Indian diaspora, the A2 desi ghee and milk market has particular resonance. NRI consumers in the US, UK, and Gulf have driven demand for premium Indian dairy products — brands like Two Brothers Organic Farms already export A2 ghee internationally. The Jains' story illustrates the kind of first-generation agricultural entrepreneurship that is making indigenous dairy commercially viable at a scale that was unthinkable a decade ago.
